name: 12-ospf-srlinux
description:
The OSPF ring of lab 11 with **Nokia SR Linux** routers: the same network, configured the way a data-centre switch is.

| Router | LAN | to the next router | to the previous router |
|---|---|---|---|
| r1 | `ethernet-1/1` `192.168.1.1/24` | `ethernet-1/2` `10.0.12.1/24` → r2 | `ethernet-1/3` `10.0.13.1/24` → r3 |
| r2 | `ethernet-1/1` `192.168.2.1/24` | `ethernet-1/3` `10.0.23.2/24` → r3 | `ethernet-1/2` `10.0.12.2/24` → r1 |
| r3 | `ethernet-1/1` `192.168.3.1/24` | `ethernet-1/3` `10.0.13.3/24` → r1 | `ethernet-1/2` `10.0.23.3/24` → r2 |

pc1, pc2 and pc3 are `192.168.1.10`, `192.168.2.10` and `192.168.3.10`, on switches sw1, sw2 and sw3. Each PC's default gateway is its router's `.1`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> SR Linux is a full network operating system: the image is about 2.5 GB, each router takes a minute or two to boot, and each uses over 1 GB of memory. Give the Docker host (GNS3 VM) at least 8 GB of RAM and 4 vCPUs for this lab.

In this lab, SR Linux configures its own interfaces, so DockerLab only names them (`e1-1` is SR Linux's `ethernet-1/1`) and leaves them without addresses. See *Network OS* in a router's settings.

## Before you start
**Deploy**, wait a couple of minutes, then open a router's **Console** and start SR Linux's CLI:
```
sr_cli
```
If it says the system isn't ready, wait a little and try again. `show interface brief` lists the interfaces.

## Configure interfaces and OSPF
In `sr_cli`, enter candidate mode, set the configuration, and commit. On **r1**:
```
enter candidate
set / interface ethernet-1/1 admin-state enable
set / interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set / interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 192.168.1.1/24
set / interface ethernet-1/2 admin-state enable
set / interface ethernet-1/2 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set / interface ethernet-1/2 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 10.0.12.1/24
set / interface ethernet-1/3 admin-state enable
set / interface ethernet-1/3 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set / interface ethernet-1/3 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 10.0.13.1/24
set / network-instance default type default
set / network-instance default admin-state enable
set / network-instance default interface ethernet-1/1.0
set / network-instance default interface ethernet-1/2.0
set / network-instance default interface ethernet-1/3.0
set / network-instance default protocols ospf instance default admin-state enable
set / network-instance default protocols ospf instance default version ospf-v2
set / network-instance default protocols ospf instance default router-id 1.1.1.1
set / network-instance default protocols ospf instance default area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/1.0 passive true
set / network-instance default protocols ospf instance default area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/2.0 interface-type point-to-point
set / network-instance default protocols ospf instance default area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/3.0 interface-type point-to-point
commit now
```
Do **r2** and **r3** the same way, with their addresses from the table and router-ids `2.2.2.2` and `3.3.3.3`.

> [!TIP]
> The configuration is saved with `save startup`, and comes back when the router stops and starts. A Redeploy starts from the factory configuration.

## Verify
1. In `sr_cli` on each router:
   ```
   show network-instance default protocols ospf neighbor
   show network-instance default route-table ipv4-unicast summary
   ping 192.168.3.10 network-instance default -c 3
   ```
2. From pc1: `ping -c 3 192.168.2.10` and `traceroute -n 192.168.3.10`.
3. Capture the **r1–r2** cable: the OSPF hellos look the same as FRR's in lab 11.

## Questions
- [ ] Compare the FRR and SR Linux configurations. What does SR Linux's *network-instance* correspond to in FRR?
- [ ] SR Linux applies nothing until `commit`. What's the advantage over FRR, where each line takes effect at once?
- [ ] Shut ethernet-1/3 on r1 (`set / interface ethernet-1/3 admin-state disable`, then `commit now`). How does traffic from pc1 reach pc3 now?

nodes.name: pc1
nodes.startup:
# r1 is the way out of this LAN
ip route replace default via 192.168.1.1
echo nameserver 1.1.1.1 > /etc/resolv.conf

nodes.name: pc2
nodes.startup:
# r2 is the way out of this LAN
ip route replace default via 192.168.2.1
echo nameserver 1.1.1.1 > /etc/resolv.conf

nodes.name: pc3
nodes.startup:
# r3 is the way out of this LAN
ip route replace default via 192.168.3.1
echo nameserver 1.1.1.1 > /etc/resolv.conf
